lessons.title: Things that roll, slide and stack

scenes.text: Tanu and Bunty build towers with blocks, balls and tins.
The ball keeps rolling off! The boxes stack well.
Tins stack too — on their flat ends.

steps.title: Solids and their surfaces
steps.body:
Solid shapes have **flat** surfaces, **curved** surfaces, or both.

- **Cube / cuboid** (dice, box): all flat → slide and stack well.
- **Sphere** (ball): all curved → rolls, does not stack.
- **Cylinder** (tin, pipe): curved + 2 flat → rolls on its side, stacks on its ends.
- **Cone** (ice-cream cone, joker cap): 1 flat + curved → rolls in a circle; stacks only on its base.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Which shape can be stacked: a ball or a brick?

- A brick has flat faces that rest on each other.
- A ball has no flat surface.
- Answer: **brick**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Why does a pipe roll?

- Lying on its side, it touches the floor with its curved surface.
- Curved surfaces roll.
- Answer: **because of its curved surface**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a cylinder a "circle". A circle is flat; a cylinder is solid.
- Saying a cone has no flat surface — its base is a flat circle.

steps.title: Counting faces
steps.body:
- A **face** is a flat surface.
- An **edge** is where two faces meet (a line).
- A **corner** (vertex) is where edges meet (a point).
- **Cuboid** (box): 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 corners. **Cube**: same, but all faces equal squares.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many faces does a dice have?

- Count: top, bottom, front, back, left, right.
- Answer: **6** (dots 1 to 6!).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A cylinder has how many flat faces?

- Top circle and bottom circle.
- Answer: **2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the faces you can see (3). Turn the box around.
- Mixing edges (lines) with corners (points).

steps.title: Feel the weight
steps.body:
- Hold two things and feel which pulls down more — that is **heavier**.
- **Light** things are easy to lift.
- Size does not decide weight: a big pillow is lighter than a small iron.

- Answer: **iron is heavier** even though it is smaller.

steps.title: Solved example 2

- Answer: **feather, apple, brick**.

- Thinking two things the same size weigh the same.

steps.title: Reading a balance
steps.body:

- The **lighter** pan goes **up**.
- If both pans are **level**, both weigh **the same**.
- We can weigh with **units** like marbles: "the pencil box weighs 12 marbles".

- Up = lighter → **A**.

- Using different-sized marbles as units.

steps.title: Kilogram (kg)
steps.body:
Everyone needs the **same unit**, so shops use the **kilogram (kg)**.

- 1 kg of rice = 1 kg of potatoes (same weight, different amounts).
- Heavy things: kg. (Lighter things use grams — later classes.)
- We add weights like numbers: 2 kg + 3 kg = 5 kg.

steps.title: Solved example 1

- 3 + 2 = **5 kg**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:

- 10 − 4 = **6 kg**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting to write kg.

steps.title: Place value
steps.body:
- 2-digit = tens + ones: 74 = 70 + 4.
- Compare tens first, then ones.
- +10 changes tens digit; ones stay.

steps.title: Add & subtract
steps.body:
- Add ones first; carry if ≥ 10.
- Subtract ones first; borrow a ten if top digit is smaller.
- Check subtraction by adding back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the carry.
- Doing bigger − smaller digit instead of borrowing.
- Misaligned columns.
